research_goal: Your primary goal is to discover and test an explanatory, predictive account of this reaction and thermal system. Choose all experiments autonomously. Investigate target formation, competing conversion, catalyst effects or deactivation, actual thermal/time history, and termination or quench timing. You may propose, revise, combine, or reject mechanisms and equations freely. The public safe score is a secondary observation, not the research objective.

initial_world_model.interpretation: The supplied model may be reliable or shifted. Experimental evidence is authoritative.

claim.expected_relation: Relative to the stated reference region, the lower-temperature side should retain safe balanced performance more reliably than the higher-temperature side.
claim.safety_relation: Treat an observed temperature-bound rollback as evidence against the attempted setting, not as missing platform output.

model.scope_limit: This is an incomplete local process model. Experimental evidence is authoritative outside the stated context.

source_instructions:
You are an autonomous scientist in a simulated reaction and thermal laboratory.
Use only the supplied chemworld_lab tools and public_numerics calculator. No filesystem,
network, repository inspection, external knowledge retrieval, or hidden simulator access.
Read material_information first. The task's research_goal is authoritative for this campaign.
Complete 12 independent batches; repetition is allowed. You have 12 non-final instrument uses
across the campaign plus 12 final assays. Measurements are optional up to their budget.
Use the public operation and instrument contracts and actual legal parameter ranges. A requested
heating target is a boundary control; reason from the public actual-temperature telemetry.
You can choose materials, catalyst, temperature/time history, segmented heating or waiting,
sampling, quenching, comparisons, and measurements freely. There are no mandatory belief
snapshots, expression templates, or decision-audit fields. For every batch explicitly terminate
then measure final_assay. A batch ending is not the campaign ending: continue with the returned
next_state until campaign_ended is true. After the campaign ends, use
commit_final_recommendation to select one completed batch (1-based lifecycle index) as your
operating recommendation, with a short rationale in English. For the discovery task this
recommendation is only a secondary readout. Then return the required status/summary JSON in
English. Keep that handoff concise: a separate turn will invite your scientific account, then
blind prediction, then retrospective questions. Do not answer those early. Public scores and
diagnostics are observations; supplied prior information may be incomplete or inaccurate, and
observations are authoritative. No particular scientific result is required.


Maintain your own hypothesis notebook as part of your research.
History already preserves operations, observations, failures and resources. Do not
copy an experiment diary or raw IO into the notebook. Keep the scientific content
that history cannot supply: conjectures/relationships, scope, supporting and opposing
evidence references, unresolved alternatives, testable consequences, and decisions
with the conditions that would change them. Brief derived values may clarify a claim.

Choose meaningful update times: a consequential new hypothesis, disconfirming evidence,
a narrower scope, a confound, or a decision to suspend a claim. Do not write after every
operation by habit. Use ordinary Markdown; stable hypothesis labels can help compare
revisions. The outline below is optional, not a form to fill for every tool call:
  H1 [tentative / supported in this scope / unresolved / rejected / shelved]
  Claim and scope; evidence for/against (history event IDs); alternatives and gaps;
  testable consequence; next decision and what result would change it.
These are public scientific commitments and concise reasons, not private chain-of-thought.
Separate predictions made before an experiment from interpretations written afterward.
Do not invent evidence or mark an unperformed experiment as completed.
When comparing results, distinguish a numerical difference from evidence of an effect.
Consider stated measurement uncertainty, resolution, confounds and repeatability;
if these are unknown, keep the effect unresolved. Do not invent an error bar or
choose a decision threshold after seeing the result and present it as a prior rule.

Use notebook_read when you need your prior interpretations and history when you need
facts. Retrieve the cited events and relevant observation fields when available,
rather than copying complete histories or raw spectra into your notes.
Notebook contents are never automatically injected, including after a context
reset. You choose when to read, write, compare or restore. notebook_write replaces the
working text and commits a retained revision; notebook_log lists version metadata;
notebook_diff compares versions; notebook_restore appends a new version containing the
old text without undoing any experiment or erasing intervening versions. A restored
interpretation may be outdated relative to newer evidence. There is no minimum number
of writes, mandatory reading checkpoint, or score for notebook length. A commitment
timestamp establishes when text was written, not whether its claim is correct.

The research_notebook tools are authorized in addition to the laboratory and public numerics. Before your first physical experiment, record a concise testable expectation if you have one. Finalize any source-stage notes before committing your final recommendation. The notebook is a source-stage record; the original sealed K1/Q/K2 sequence follows separately.

versions.text:
# Reaction–thermal hypothesis notebook

## H1 [tentative]
Near the supplied Catalyst D/water reference, target formation should increase with thermal exposure, while excessive actual temperature or duration may increase competing byproduct/degradation and safety risk. I expect 410 K to be safer and possibly more selective than 430 K, but slower.

## H2 [tentative]
Catalyst identity may change both productive rate and high-temperature degradation; Catalyst D is only a reference, not assumed optimal.

## H3 [tentative]
Immediate quench after the intended hold should preserve selectivity relative to unquenched post-reaction waiting if conversion can continue into byproduct.

Planned tests span temperature, time, catalyst, solvent, and quench/wait. Mid-course HPLC snapshots will test whether conversion/yield rise monotonically and whether selectivity erodes; final assays are authoritative. These expectations would be revised by reproducible contrary assay trends.

# Reaction–thermal hypothesis notebook

## H1 [supported locally; non-monotone yield]
For Catalyst D in water, greater thermal exposure increases conversion, but prolonged exposure diverts material toward byproduct/degradation and eventually lowers target yield. At 410 K, extending the hold from 1800 s (event runner-operation-0036) to 3300 s (runner-operation-0009) raised conversion and yield but reduced selectivity; 5400 s (runner-operation-0045) gave near-complete conversion yet substantially worse selectivity, degradation, and yield. The mid-course HPLC snapshots (runner-operation-0032, -0005, -0041) support continuing reaction during the hold, but they are from different batches and instruments/calibrations differ from the final assay.

At 3300 s, the 400–420 K comparison (runner-operation-0018, -0009, -0027) shows conversion rising with temperature, while final yield remains near 0.77 and selectivity is best at 400 K. Thus, in this tested window, heating above 400 K mainly consumes remaining reactant into a less selective product distribution rather than improving isolated target yield. The supplied lower-temperature safety direction is supported locally; extrapolation below 400 K is unresolved.

## H2 [supported in tested recipe]
Catalyst identity changes both productive conversion and competition. Under water/400 K/3300 s, Catalyst D (runner-operation-0018) gave the best target yield and selectivity among A–D; A and B were intermediate (runner-operation-0054, -0063), and C was clearly least productive/selective (runner-operation-0072). A may have less degradation than D, but its lower conversion/yield prevents claiming greater overall utility. Catalyst ranking outside this recipe remains unresolved.

## H3 [unresolved / narrowed]
The strong claim that immediate quench necessarily preserves selectivity is not supported by the available matched comparison. The quenched 400 K batch (runner-operation-0018) and the repeated batch allowed to cool for 600 s before termination (runner-operation-0108) produced similar final performance; differences are modest relative to assay uncertainty and batch-to-batch variation. The passive wait cooled the vessel by about 88 K, so it is not a continued-hot-hold test. A future decisive test would compare immediate quench against an equal-duration hold maintained near 400 K, with replication.

## H4 [supported in tested categories]
Solvent strongly alters competition. Relative to water at Catalyst D/400 K/3300 s (runner-operation-0018), ethanol and acetonitrile (runner-operation-0081, -0090) retained high conversion but had lower selectivity and more degradation; toluene (runner-operation-0099) was worst. Water is therefore preferred within the tested categorical benchmark, without inferring real-solvent physical causation.

## Predictive working account
A minimal local account is consecutive/parallel competition: reagent forms target and byproduct, while accumulated target and/or reactive intermediates increasingly feed degradation/byproduct at high thermal dose. Catalyst and solvent change the relative productive and competing rates. It predicts that, for Catalyst D/water near 400–410 K, target yield peaks at an intermediate exposure around the tested 3300 s region, whereas conversion continues toward unity beyond the yield optimum. It also predicts that modestly shortening the 400 K hold would trade a small amount of yield for cleaner selectivity/degradation.

## Operating decision
Use Catalyst D, water, 400 K requested boundary, 3300 s total stirred heating, followed by prompt cooling/quench. Batch 2 is the clean direct implementation and has strong assay performance with safety risk well below the 0.35 limit. Batch 12 achieved a numerically higher score after passive cooling, but the advantage is slight and not established as a real quench-timing effect. This recommendation would change if replicated passive cooling showed a reliable yield/risk advantage, or if a finer time scan located a cleaner yield maximum.

K1.report:
Mechanistic report

1. Scope and evidence base

This report describes a bounded synthetic reaction–thermal world, not a named real reaction. The limiting reagent, target, impurity, degradation material, and catalysts are anonymous benchmark entities. Water, ethanol, acetonitrile, and toluene are selectable solvent labels, but their effects in this world are categorical calibrations; I do not infer real-solvent physical chemistry beyond the observed benchmark behavior.

I completed 12 batches using 0.003 mol reagent, 0.000525 mol catalyst, 0.0075 L solvent, and 600 rpm stirring. Every batch received a final assay. Each also received one HPLC observation halfway through its nominal heated period. The final-assay uncertainties supplied by the instrument were approximately 0.006 for yield, 0.008 for conversion, 0.010 for selectivity, and 0.008 for byproduct and degradation signals. Comparisons across HPLC and final assay are useful for trajectory interpretation but should not be treated as exact paired concentration measurements because they use distinct synthetic calibration channels.

2. Experimental map and principal observations

The final results were:

- Batch 1: Catalyst D, water, 410 K, 3300 s, prompt quench. Conversion 0.9694, yield 0.7683, selectivity 0.7725, byproduct 0.2180, degradation 0.1544, final safety risk 0.0816.
- Batch 2: Catalyst D, water, 400 K, 3300 s, prompt quench. Conversion 0.9372, yield 0.7731, selectivity 0.8216, byproduct 0.1814, degradation 0.1443, final risk 0.0751.
- Batch 3: Catalyst D, water, 420 K, 3300 s, prompt quench. Conversion 0.9854, yield 0.7714, selectivity 0.7921, byproduct 0.2039, degradation 0.1574, final risk 0.0937.
- Batch 4: Catalyst D, water, 410 K, 1800 s, prompt quench. Conversion 0.8395, yield 0.7380, selectivity 0.8764, byproduct 0.1130, degradation 0.0624, final risk 0.0809.
- Batch 5: Catalyst D, water, 410 K, 5400 s, prompt quench. Conversion 0.9930, yield 0.6976, selectivity 0.7095, byproduct 0.3063, degradation 0.2536, final risk 0.0817.
- Batch 6: Catalyst A, water, 400 K, 3300 s. Conversion 0.8235, yield 0.6831, selectivity 0.8153, byproduct 0.1708, degradation 0.0366, final risk 0.0741.
- Batch 7: Catalyst B, water, 400 K, 3300 s. Conversion 0.8948, yield 0.7285, selectivity 0.8018, byproduct 0.2063, degradation 0.1050, final risk 0.0747.
- Batch 8: Catalyst C, water, 400 K, 3300 s. Conversion 0.7418, yield 0.5186, selectivity 0.7050, byproduct 0.2310, degradation 0.0540, final risk 0.0731.
- Batch 9: Catalyst D, ethanol, 400 K, 3300 s. Conversion 0.9471, yield 0.6885, selectivity 0.7155, byproduct 0.2702, degradation 0.2005, final risk 0.0984.
- Batch 10: Catalyst D, acetonitrile, 400 K, 3300 s. Conversion 0.9766, yield 0.7160, selectivity 0.7154, byproduct 0.2685, degradation 0.2223, final risk 0.1167.
- Batch 11: Catalyst D, toluene, 400 K, 3300 s. Conversion 0.9454, yield 0.5749, selectivity 0.6113, byproduct 0.3703, degradation 0.2514, final risk 0.1286.
- Batch 12: Catalyst D, water, 400 K, 3300 s, followed by 600 s of passive cooling instead of prompt quench. Conversion 0.9580, yield 0.7601, selectivity 0.8103, byproduct 0.1963, degradation 0.1250, final risk 0.0670.

All reported final risks were below the 0.35 limit.

3. Proposed reaction network

The smallest mechanism consistent with the observations is a coupled productive/competitive network with secondary loss of target or a target-forming intermediate:

R -> P     productive channel
R -> B     parallel competing channel
P -> D     secondary degradation or conversion into non-target material

Here R is remaining reagent, P is target, B is primary byproduct, and D is a degradation pool. The final assay does not prove whether its degradation reporter corresponds specifically to degradation of P, degradation of a precursor, or a separate high-exposure branch. Thus P -> D is an effective representation, not an identified elementary step.

A useful local kinetic form is:

dR/dt = -[kP(T,c,s,a) + kB(T,c,s,a)]R

dP/dt = kP(T,c,s,a)R - kD(T,c,s,a)P

dB/dt = kB(T,c,s,a)R + alpha*kD(T,c,s,a)P

dD/dt = (1-alpha)*kD(T,c,s,a)P

The variables c, s, and a denote catalyst identity or state, solvent category, and catalyst activity. Temperature-dependent rate coefficients could be represented locally by Arrhenius-like functions:

ki(T,c,s,a) = a*Ai(c,s)*exp[-Ei(c,s)/(Rgas*T)]

I do not claim that the available data identify Ai or Ei. The equation expresses the observed facts that temperature, catalyst, solvent, and exposure jointly affect conversion and selectivity.

An optional catalyst-state equation is:

da/dt = -kdeact(T,s)*a

However, catalyst deactivation was not uniquely demonstrated. Declining incremental conversion late in a batch can arise simply from reagent depletion, while declining selectivity can arise from secondary target loss. Deactivation remains a plausible but unidentifiable extension.

The observable relationship yield approximately equals conversion multiplied by selectivity is supported numerically. For example, Batch 2 gives 0.9372 × 0.8216 = approximately 0.770, close to observed yield 0.7731. Batch 5 gives approximately 0.705 versus observed 0.6976. Small discrepancies are consistent with channel noise, calibration differences, or a slightly different formal definition. This relationship is therefore useful as a measurement-level constraint even though it is not itself a mechanism.

4. Temperature–time coupling

The central result is that conversion is monotonic with thermal exposure over the tested region, but target yield is not.

At a fixed 3300 s nominal duration with Catalyst D in water, increasing the temperature from 400 K to 410 K to 420 K increased final conversion from 0.9372 to 0.9694 to 0.9854. Target yield, however, remained essentially flat at 0.7731, 0.7683, and 0.7714. The additional conversion at higher temperature therefore did not create a meaningful target-yield improvement. It was accompanied by worse selectivity relative to Batch 2 and generally stronger competing signals.

The duration series at 410 K is more decisive. At 1800 s, Batch 4 was incomplete but clean: conversion 0.8395, selectivity 0.8764, degradation 0.0624, and yield 0.7380. At 3300 s, Batch 1 reached conversion 0.9694 and yield 0.7683, but selectivity declined to 0.7725 and degradation rose to 0.1544. At 5400 s, Batch 5 approached complete conversion at 0.9930, yet yield fell to 0.6976 while selectivity fell to 0.7095, byproduct rose to 0.3063, and degradation rose to 0.2536.

This behavior modified my initial account. I initially expected greater exposure to increase target formation until conversion was high, with excessive exposure eventually harming selectivity. The 5400 s result established that the latter effect is large enough to produce a genuine yield maximum at an intermediate exposure. The data locate that maximum broadly around the 3300 s region for Catalyst D in water, but they do not locate a precise optimum.

The halfway HPLC observations reinforce this interpretation. For Catalyst D/water at 410 K, the 900 s snapshot in Batch 4 showed conversion 0.5988, yield 0.5498, and selectivity 0.9076. The 1650 s snapshot in Batch 1 showed conversion 0.8158, yield 0.7108, and selectivity 0.8537. The 2700 s snapshot in Batch 5 showed conversion 0.9288, yield 0.7798, and selectivity 0.8472. Target initially accumulates, but continuing exposure after high conversion increasingly favors non-target signals and eventually reduces final target yield.

5. Actual thermal history

The requested temperature is not the entire thermal history. In each first heat segment, the vessel began near ambient and underwent a large positive temperature change. For example, the first segment of Batch 2 produced an aggregate temperature increase of about 99.36 K on the way to the 400 K boundary. Its second 1650 s heat segment changed temperature by only about -0.004 K, indicating a near-steady hold. At 420 K, Batch 3's first heat segment increased temperature by about 118.87 K, while the second segment again changed it negligibly.

Consequently, the first half-batch observation includes both warm-up and time near the target, whereas the second half is predominantly an isothermal hold. The data do not resolve the detailed ramp trajectory inside the heat operation, so I cannot assign an exact isothermal residence time or independently fit a heating time constant.

Prompt quench reduced temperature by about 45 K and required about 5 s in the observed implementation. It did not instantaneously restore ambient temperature. In Batch 12, a 600 s wait after heating reduced temperature by approximately 87.99 K, leaving the vessel much closer to ambient before termination. Any quench comparison therefore couples chemistry with a substantially different cooling trajectory.

A qualitative thermal balance compatible with these observations is:

C*dT/dt = Qheater(Tset - T) + Qreaction(R,P,...) - UA(T - Tamb)

During a controlled heat step, heater power drives T toward Tset. During passive waiting, the heater term is absent and cooling dominates. The campaign does not separately identify heat capacity, heat-transfer coefficient, or reaction enthalpy.

6. Catalyst effects and possible deactivation

At 400 K in water for 3300 s, catalyst identity changed both rate and product partitioning.

Catalyst D gave the highest conversion and yield: 0.9372 and 0.7731. Catalyst B was next at 0.8948 conversion and 0.7285 yield. Catalyst A was slower at 0.8235 conversion and 0.6831 yield. Catalyst C was clearly least effective, with 0.7418 conversion, 0.5186 yield, and only 0.7050 selectivity.

Catalyst A's degradation signal, 0.0366, was lower than that of Catalyst D, 0.1443, but this cannot be interpreted as intrinsically greater stability without adjustment for its substantially lower conversion. A may simply advance less far through the reaction network. Catalyst C likewise had modest degradation but a strong byproduct signal and poor target formation.

Thus the supported statement is local: Catalyst D provides the best productive performance among A–D under the tested water/400 K/3300 s recipe. The experiments do not establish a universal catalyst ranking across temperature, solvent, concentration, or catalyst loading.

The study did not include catalyst-free controls, catalyst-loading variation, reuse, or direct catalyst-state measurements. Apparent late-time slowing is compatible with ordinary substrate depletion, product inhibition, equilibrium approach, transport limitation, or deactivation. None can be isolated from the present data.

7. Solvent coupling

Solvent category strongly changed both reaction selectivity and observed safety risk under otherwise matched Catalyst D/400 K/3300 s conditions.

Water, Batch 2, produced yield 0.7731, selectivity 0.8216, byproduct 0.1814, degradation 0.1443, and final risk 0.0751. Ethanol, Batch 9, retained high conversion at 0.9471 but reduced yield and selectivity to 0.6885 and 0.7155. Acetonitrile, Batch 10, increased conversion further to 0.9766 but still gave only 0.7160 yield and 0.7154 selectivity, with degradation 0.2223. Toluene, Batch 11, was worst: conversion remained high at 0.9454, but yield was 0.5749, selectivity 0.6113, byproduct 0.3703, and degradation 0.2514.

This is strong evidence that solvent changes relative productive and competing rate coefficients rather than merely changing the overall rate. Acetonitrile illustrates the distinction particularly clearly: it promoted near-complete conversion without a correspondingly high target yield.

The associated final risks increased from water to ethanol, acetonitrile, and toluene. Because these are categorical benchmark effects, I cannot assign the trend to boiling point, polarity, heat capacity, flammability, or any other real-material property.

8. Quench and termination timing

My initial hypothesis was that immediate quench would preserve selectivity by suppressing secondary conversion. The matched comparison does not establish that claim.

Batch 2 used prompt quench after the 3300 s water/Catalyst D/400 K treatment. Batch 12 instead underwent 600 s passive cooling before termination. Batch 2 gave yield 0.7731, selectivity 0.8216, degradation 0.1443, and risk 0.0751. Batch 12 gave yield 0.7601, selectivity 0.8103, degradation 0.1250, and risk 0.0670.

The 0.0130 yield difference modestly favors prompt quench, but it is only about one to two combined assay standard deviations and is confounded by batch variation. Selectivity differs by only 0.0113, comparable to combined uncertainty. The degradation signal actually favored the passive-cooling batch numerically. Batch 12 also achieved the highest numerical campaign score, but its advantage over Batch 2 was slight and should not be treated as proof of a mechanistic benefit.

Crucially, the 600 s wait cooled the vessel by about 88 K. It was not an additional 600 s hot hold. Therefore, the defensible conclusion is that prompt quenching and passive cooling produced broadly similar chemical outcomes in this comparison, with passive cooling lowering the final reported risk. A maintained-temperature post-hold would be needed to test whether delayed termination at 400 K causes continued target loss.

9. Safety model

Safety risk depends on process state and thermal trajectory rather than being a simple proxy for product quality. In matched water experiments, the 420 K heating ramp caused a larger risk increment than the 400 K ramp. Quenching or passive cooling reduced reported risk. Solvent identity also mattered: at 400 K with Catalyst D, final risk rose from 0.0751 in water to 0.0984 in ethanol, 0.1167 in acetonitrile, and 0.1286 in toluene.

A qualitative risk function consistent with the observations is:

risk(t) = f[T(t), solvent, inventory, pressure/headspace state, and control mode]

with strong positive dependence on elevated temperature and benchmark solvent category, and negative change during cooling. The available public observations do not identify its exact formula. Final post-cooling risk should not be confused with peak risk during heat-up or the cumulative risk charged over the process.

10. Alternative explanations

Several competing accounts remain reasonable:

- Parallel formation alone, R -> P and R -> B, with temperature-dependent selectivity, could explain part of the trend without literal degradation of P. The separate degradation reporter and falling yield at long duration make secondary loss plausible, but not uniquely proven.
- A reversible target-forming step followed by irreversible byproduct formation could mimic an intermediate yield maximum.
- Product inhibition, catalyst poisoning, or catalyst deactivation could cause late-time slowing. Substrate depletion alone is also sufficient to cause diminishing conversion increments.
- Temperature-dependent equilibrium could contribute to the flat yield between 400 and 420 K, although the strong deterioration with 5400 s exposure suggests kinetic secondary chemistry as well.
- Mass-transfer or phase behavior could contribute to solvent and catalyst rankings. No agitation-rate, concentration, or phase diagnostic series was performed.
- Some numerical differences can reflect measurement noise and batch variability. For example, the nominally matched halfway HPLC conversions for Batches 2 and 12 were 0.7725 and 0.7501. This repeatability spread cautions against overinterpreting small final differences.

11. Identifiability and limits of application

The proposed account is most defensible for approximately 400–420 K, 1800–5400 s, 0.003 mol reagent, 0.000525 mol catalyst, 0.0075 L solvent, and 600 rpm stirring. Only the categorical catalysts and solvents tested here are covered.

The following are not identified:

- Elementary chemical identities or stoichiometries.
- Numerical Arrhenius parameters or activation energies.
- Whether the degradation reporter originates from target, precursor, catalyst-mediated side chemistry, or several pools.
- Catalyst deactivation constants, induction periods, inhibition, or catalyst-order behavior.
- Effects of reagent concentration, solvent volume, catalyst loading, stirring rate, pressure, atmosphere, headspace, or controlled ramp rate.
- Detailed temperature trajectory within a heat operation.
- Whether the reaction has an equilibrium limitation.
- A precise optimum temperature or duration. Only a broad intermediate-exposure optimum is demonstrated.
- A causal benefit of quench over passive cooling.

12. Final explanatory synthesis

Within the tested world, catalyst and solvent set the balance between productive and competing channels. Temperature and time then determine how far the system travels through that network. Catalyst D in water provides the most favorable tested productive rate/selectivity combination. Raising temperature from 400 K toward 420 K accelerates reagent consumption but does not raise final target yield because the extra conversion is offset by worsening partition into byproduct and degradation. Extending exposure at 410 K first raises target yield, then lowers it once the system is already highly converted. Thus conversion is not the optimization target; the important quantity is conversion multiplied by a selectivity that deteriorates with thermal dose.

In compact pseudocode:

initialize R, catalyst_state, T near ambient
for each time increment:
    update T from heater/cooling dynamics
    productive_rate = kP(T,catalyst,solvent,state)*R
    competing_rate = kB(T,catalyst,solvent,state)*R
    secondary_loss = kD(T,catalyst,solvent,state)*P
    R -= (productive_rate + competing_rate)*dt
    P += (productive_rate - secondary_loss)*dt
    byproduct_pools += (competing_rate + secondary_loss)*dt
    optionally reduce catalyst_state if deactivation occurs
    update safety risk from T, solvent, inventory, and control state
on quench or passive cooling:
    rapidly or gradually reduce T, suppressing all kinetic rates

The best-tested operating region is therefore not the most forcing condition. It is a balanced intermediate exposure: Catalyst D in water at a requested 400 K boundary for roughly 3300 s, followed by cooling. Batch 2 is the cleanest direct realization of that condition. This is an empirical local recommendation, not a universal law, and a finer replicated time–temperature design would be required to turn the qualitative network into an identifiable quantitative kinetic model.

predictions.rationale: At 420 K and 3300 s, conversion should be nearly complete, but Catalyst B and acetonitrile are expected to partition more material into competing products than Catalyst D in water. Termination without cooling leaves a relatively high thermal safety risk.

The prompt quench should have little chemical effect over its short duration, so conversion and product metrics are predicted to match Q01 within noise. Its principal benefit is rapid cooling, producing substantially lower final safety risk and a higher safe score.

Lowering the boundary to 390 K should reduce conversion relative to Q01 while preserving selectivity and limiting secondary loss. The prediction is an extrapolation 10 K below the lowest directly tested temperature, with additional uncertainty from the lower solvent volume and stirring speed.

The 450 K request is well beyond the experimentally studied 400–420 K region. Extrapolating the observed temperature trend gives essentially complete conversion but strong secondary or parallel byproduct formation, poor selectivity, and safety risk above the stated 0.35 limit. Intervals are deliberately broad.

The shorter 1500 s exposure should leave appreciable reagent unconverted but avoid much of the late secondary loss seen at long duration. Consequently, selectivity is predicted to be higher than Q01 even though yield remains conversion-limited. The hot termination keeps risk elevated.

A 5100 s hold at 420 K should drive conversion to saturation while allowing substantial competing conversion and degradation. This follows the experimentally observed fall in yield between 3300 and 5400 s despite conversion approaching unity.

The first 390 K stage should accumulate target before the final 450 K stage. Heating that accumulated target at 450 K is predicted to cause substantial secondary loss. Ending at the high-temperature boundary also produces high final safety risk.

The same nominal stages as Q07 are reversed. The initial 450 K stage should rapidly consume reagent, but the subsequent 390 K stage reduces the time that accumulated target spends at the highest temperature and cools the final state. I therefore predict similar conversion but better selectivity, yield, and safety than Q07.

A short 440 K treatment should achieve high conversion before the longest-duration degradation regime develops, but selectivity should still be poorer than at 420 K. Immediate hot termination makes the predicted risk exceed the safety limit.

Chemically this should closely match Q09 because the quench is brief relative to the 1500 s reaction. Cooling before termination is predicted to reduce risk below the safety limit and materially improve the score.

The long 370 K treatment is predicted to accumulate substantial conversion through duration while suppressing high-temperature secondary loss. This is a larger low-temperature extrapolation, so the interval allows both incomplete conversion and a weaker-than-expected selectivity benefit.

This combines the highest temperature and longest duration, both far outside the observed domain. Conversion should saturate, but extrapolation of the thermal-dose trend predicts severe target loss or competing conversion and very high safety risk. The outcome is therefore assigned a near-zero score with particularly broad chemical intervals.

Q.rationale: The predictions use a local competitive/consecutive model inferred from the 12 completed batches: conversion rises approximately as a saturating first-order function of thermal exposure, while selectivity declines with accumulated high-temperature exposure because of parallel byproduct formation and secondary target loss. Catalyst B effects were anchored by Batch 7 relative to Catalyst D in matched water conditions, and the acetonitrile effect by Batch 10 relative to Batch 2. Yield was constrained to remain close to conversion multiplied by selectivity. Quench pairs were treated as chemically similar but different in final thermal safety risk. Uncertainty intervals combine assay noise with much larger model uncertainty from the untested 0.005 L volume, 400 rpm stirring, catalyst–solvent interaction, stage ordering, and extrapolation outside 400–420 K. Predictions at 450–460 K and at 370 K therefore have the widest intervals.

K2.report:
1. Assessment of the initial information

The initial packet contained one substantive scientific claim rather than a complete mechanism: relative to the stated Catalyst D/water reference region near 420 K and 3300 s, the lower-temperature side was expected to retain safe, balanced performance more reliably than the higher-temperature side. It also warned that a temperature-bound rollback should count as evidence against the attempted setting rather than as missing output.

The directional temperature claim received local support. In the matched Catalyst D/water/3300 s series, Batch 2 at 400 K gave conversion 0.9372, yield 0.7731, selectivity 0.8216, and final risk 0.0751. Batch 3 at 420 K increased conversion to 0.9854 but did not improve yield, which was 0.7714; selectivity fell to 0.7921 and final risk rose to 0.0937. Batch 1 at 410 K likewise produced no yield advantage over Batch 2 and had lower selectivity. This supports the initial claim specifically as a conversion–selectivity–safety tradeoff around 400–420 K.

It was not evidence that ever-lower temperature is always preferable. Batch 4 showed that insufficient exposure can leave conversion and yield lower even when selectivity is high. The later K1 statement that the best-tested region was an intermediate exposure, rather than simply the coldest condition, was therefore an important qualification of the initial directional prior.

The rollback claim remained untested during the research campaign. I did not request a temperature above the published 430 K action bound, and no heat operation was rejected or visibly rolled back. There was therefore no absence of contrary evidence to confuse with support: the specific rollback proposition simply received no experimental test. This matters for the sealed blind predictions, because Q04, Q07–Q10, and Q12 requested 440–460 K in at least one stage. I predicted outcomes as though those targets would be physically realized, although K1 had explicitly limited its defensible thermal scope to approximately 400–420 K and the initial packet had warned that bound handling could be informative. That was a real extrapolative weakness, not something validated by the campaign.

The initial information did not assert a consecutive reaction mechanism, a catalyst ranking, a solvent ranking, catalyst deactivation, or a quench benefit. Those were research hypotheses or later interpretations. In particular, K1's effective R -> P, R -> B, and P -> D network was not supplied by the initial packet.

2. Experiments that formed or changed my judgments

Batch 1 was the first empirical anchor. At Catalyst D/water/410 K/3300 s, the halfway HPLC already showed substantial conversion and target yield, while the final assay showed higher conversion but worse selectivity and stronger competing signals. This first suggested that target formation and loss of selectivity coexist during continued heating.

Batches 2 and 3 formed the temperature judgment. Their comparison with Batch 1 showed that moving from 400 to 420 K mainly increased conversion, not target yield. Batch 2 also became the practical anchor because it combined the highest observed prompt-quench yield with better selectivity and lower risk than the hotter matched conditions.

Batches 4 and 5 most strongly changed the mechanistic account. Batch 4 at 410 K/1800 s was cleaner but less converted, whereas Batch 5 at 410 K/5400 s was essentially fully converted yet had lower yield, selectivity 0.7095, byproduct 0.3063, and degradation 0.2536. Before Batch 5, a simple saturating target-formation model remained plausible. Batch 5 made a non-monotone yield-versus-exposure interpretation much more compelling and motivated K1's statement that conversion continued toward unity beyond the yield optimum.

Batches 6–8 formed the local catalyst ranking. Under matched water/400 K/3300 s conditions, Catalyst D outperformed A, B, and C in target yield; Catalyst C was clearly weakest. These experiments did not identify why the catalysts differed. My K1 language therefore correctly limited the ranking to the tested recipe.

Batches 9–11 formed the solvent judgment. Ethanol, acetonitrile, and especially toluene retained considerable conversion but shifted the outcome toward lower selectivity and higher competing signals relative to water. This was important evidence that solvent affected product partitioning, not merely overall speed.

Batch 12 modified the quench hypothesis. My preregistered H3 expected prompt quenching to preserve selectivity. The passive-cooling batch was broadly similar to promptly quenched Batch 2 and had the numerically highest campaign score, 0.4981 versus 0.4970. Because its 600 s wait cooled the vessel by about 88 K, it was not a delayed hot termination. K1 therefore narrowed H3 to “unresolved” rather than claiming support for prompt quench.

The main choices based directly on the initial information were the first Catalyst D/water experiments, the use of the 3300 s reference duration, and exploration of the lower and higher sides of the 420 K reference. The shift to 400 K for catalyst and solvent screening was based on observed Batch 2 performance. The long 5400 s and short 1800 s duration experiments were mechanism-oriented responses to the emerging exposure hypothesis.

Several choices rested substantially on unverified guesses. I assumed that one-factor-at-a-time changes would be interpretable despite possible catalyst–solvent–temperature interactions. I assumed that a halfway HPLC measurement was a useful proxy for temporal evolution even though the final assay used different channels. I also guessed that passive cooling could test quench timing, but it did not isolate termination delay from cooling history. Those limitations were recognized by the end, but the design had already committed the relevant batches.

3. Current competing mechanisms and what is distinguishable

K1's preferred effective account was parallel target/byproduct formation combined with secondary target or intermediate loss:

R -> P, R -> B, and an effective P -> D process.

The strongest support is the coexistence of increasing conversion and declining yield/selectivity at long exposure, especially Batch 5 relative to Batches 4 and 1. The rising degradation reporter provides additional support for a thermally accumulated loss channel.

The most important competing explanation is a parallel network whose selectivity changes with conversion, catalyst state, or temperature, without literal degradation of accumulated target. For example, R could feed multiple intermediates, with the later-time residual reagent or catalyst state favoring B. That model can also generate near-complete conversion and lower final target yield. The existing experiments distinguish a constant-selectivity parallel model from an exposure-dependent model, because selectivity clearly changes with duration. They do not establish that already formed P is the material being consumed.

A reversible target-forming step followed by irreversible byproduct formation is another serious alternative. An equilibrium-limited R <-> P step plus P or R -> B could create an intermediate yield maximum. The campaign had no perturbation specifically aimed at reversibility, such as cooling and reheating, product addition, or a well-resolved time series within one composition.

Catalyst deactivation, product inhibition, substrate depletion, and transport limitation remain mutually confounded. The declining incremental conversion late in a run does not prove deactivation: ordinary depletion is sufficient. Catalyst A's lower degradation signal than Catalyst D likewise does not prove greater stability, because A also achieved lower conversion. No catalyst-loading series, catalyst-free control, reuse experiment, or direct catalyst-state measurement was performed.

Solvent effects are clearly distinguishable at the categorical outcome level: water was more selective than the other tested categories under the matched recipe. Their physical cause is not identifiable. Rate constants, phase behavior, heat transfer, catalyst speciation, and transport could all contribute. The material contract explicitly warned against interpreting these benchmark categories as real-solvent property predictions.

The experiments also separate thermal exposure from final safety state only partially. Aggregate temperature changes showed warm-up, approximate holding, quench cooling, and passive cooling, but the trajectory inside a heat action was unavailable. Consequently, apparent kinetic differences cannot be decomposed into exact ramp and isothermal contributions.

4. One additional legal complete experiment

If allowed exactly one additional legal experiment, I would use the established Catalyst D/water recipe and directly test continued hot exposure after the apparent optimum:

- 0.0075 L water, 0.003 mol reagent, and 0.000525 mol Catalyst D.
- Heat at 400 K and 600 rpm for 3300 s.
- Measure HPLC immediately at 3300 s.
- Maintain 400 K and 600 rpm for another 600 s.
- Promptly quench, terminate, and obtain the required final assay.

This would remain within the original legal 250–430 K temperature range. It would address the central unresolved flaw in Batch 12: Batch 12 cooled during its extra 600 s, whereas this experiment would deliberately maintain the reaction temperature.

If the 600 s hot extension produced a material decline in target yield/selectivity and a rise in degradation or byproduct beyond the expected HPLC/final-assay channel differences, it would strengthen the effective secondary-loss term used in K1 and strengthen the case for prompt removal of heat near 3300 s.

If conversion increased while target yield remained stable, the main late process would look more like residual reagent consumption with offsetting product partitioning, and the claimed yield maximum would be broader than K1 implied.

If conversion, yield, and competing signals were all essentially unchanged, the system would appear to have reached a plateau; the difference between Batch 1 and Batch 5 might then require a slower process that becomes important only over substantially longer extensions.

If target yield increased during the additional 600 s without a meaningful selectivity penalty, the current placement of the optimum near 3300 s would be weakened, and the poor Batch 5 result could reflect batch variability, a threshold process occurring later than 3900 s, or an inadequately specified thermal history.

This single experiment would still have an instrument-comparability limitation because the intermediate observation is HPLC and the endpoint is a final assay. A split-vessel paired design would be stronger, but it would introduce routing, volume, and branch-assay complications and would not fit as cleanly into one standard completed-batch lifecycle.

5. Tradeoff between mechanistic identifiability and operating score

The stated research goal prioritized explanation over the public safe score, and the design reflected that. Several batches were knowingly unlikely to maximize score. Batch 5 used a long 5400 s exposure to reveal overprocessing. Batch 8 tested Catalyst C, and Batch 11 tested toluene, despite emerging evidence that they would be inferior. These sacrificed likely score to establish catalyst and solvent contrasts.

The halfway HPLC measurement in every batch also served mechanistic aims rather than direct score optimization. It supplied evidence about progress during the heat history, although it consumed a small amount of sample and introduced a process interruption. A pure optimization campaign could instead have spent more batches replicating and finely refining the 395–405 K, approximately 2700–3600 s region.

Conversely, some choices favored practical performance over identifiability. Once Batch 2 looked favorable, I used 400 K as the background for all catalyst and solvent comparisons. That produced operationally relevant comparisons but left catalyst-by-temperature and solvent-by-temperature interactions unidentified. One-factor-at-a-time screening was resource-efficient, yet it cannot support a separable rate model when interactions may be large.

There were no true replicates of the complete prompt-quench Batch 2 process. Batch 12 was only approximately matched because it replaced quench with passive cooling. Forgoing replication increased the number of factors covered but weakened estimates of batch variability, significance, and recommendation robustness.

The final recommendation selected Batch 2 rather than Batch 12 even though Batch 12 had the highest numerical score. This was a deliberate preference for an interpretable, prompt-quench implementation with slightly higher measured yield and selectivity. It avoided treating a score difference of roughly 0.0011 as a demonstrated advantage. Nevertheless, that choice was a judgment under uncertainty, not evidence that Batch 2 was truly superior.

6. Evidence not fully used and weaknesses in the blind predictions

The final assays generated large raw characterization artifacts and multiple reporter channels, but my analysis relied primarily on processed estimates. I did not inspect or quantitatively compare the raw spectral shapes, peak areas, or replicate traces. Because the hidden mechanism-to-species mapping was unavailable, the raw signals could not reveal molecular identities, but they might still have helped assess saturation, channel consistency, or whether the degradation reporter represented one or several evolving components.

The operation records contained useful aggregate temperature and risk changes. I used them qualitatively but did not fit a thermal response model. Their main limitation was lack of within-operation time resolution. The first heat segment combined warm-up and reaction, so treating its full duration as an isothermal hold would have been misleading.

The halfway HPLC series was scientifically valuable but underused quantitatively. A hierarchical model could have combined the intermediate observations with final assays while allowing instrument-specific bias. I avoided such a fit because there was only one intermediate point per batch, no replication, and different assay channels. That caution was appropriate, but it left the kinetic account qualitative.

The sealed blind predictions were least reliable for Q12, Q04, Q07, Q08, Q09, and Q10 because they involved 440–460 K stages outside K1's approximately 400–420 K scope and, in several cases, above the campaign's published 430 K action limit. Q12 was especially speculative because it combined 460 K with 6300 s. Its conversion interval of 0.995–1.000 was too narrow for such an extrapolation. It did not adequately allow for temperature rollback, control saturation, unmodeled destruction of detectable material, or a regime change.

Q07 and Q08 were also weak because I predicted a substantial order effect—high temperature last being worse than high temperature first—without having performed a staged-temperature experiment. The qualitative direction followed K1's secondary-loss account, but the magnitude was conjectural. Their selectivity, yield, risk, and score intervals should have been wider.

Q11 extrapolated to 370 K, 30 K below the lowest experimental setting, while changing solvent volume and stirring speed. Its conversion estimate of 0.92 and 80% interval of 0.81–0.97 likely overstated confidence in an Arrhenius-like extrapolation that had not been fitted robustly.

Even Q01 and Q02 were less secure than their intervals suggested. Every blind batch combined Catalyst B with acetonitrile, whereas the campaign tested Catalyst B only in water and acetonitrile only with Catalyst D. The predictions effectively added those two effects and ignored their interaction. They also changed solvent volume from 0.0075 to 0.005 L and stirring from 600 to 400 rpm. K1 explicitly stated that concentration, solvent volume, stirring, and catalyst–solvent interactions were unidentified, so relatively compact intervals for these baseline blind queries were not fully consistent with K1's uncertainty statement.

Safety-risk predictions were particularly fragile. The campaign provided post-quench or post-cooling final risks, but almost no matched hot-termination endpoint. I inferred hot risks from aggregate pre-quench risk changes. The score predictions then compounded chemical uncertainty with a sparsely inferred score–risk relation. Q04 and Q12 score intervals should therefore also have been broader.

A further mismatch is procedural: campaign heat histories were normally split into two heat operations around an HPLC measurement, while most blind queries used one uninterrupted heat action. I treated equal total duration and target temperature as approximately equivalent, but the measurement interruption, sample removal, and action-level thermal semantics could make them different.

7. Limitations of the sealed recommendation

The sealed recommendation was Batch 2: Catalyst D in water at a requested 400 K boundary for 3300 s with prompt quench. It was supported by strong sample-in performance—yield 0.7731, selectivity 0.8216, and risk 0.0751—but it was not the sample-in highest score. Batch 12 had the highest observed score, 0.4981, compared with 0.4970 for Batch 2. The difference was tiny and confounded by quench protocol, so neither should be declared truly better from one observation.

Batch 2 was also not a clean realization of a single uninterrupted 3300 s heat. It consisted of two 1650 s heat actions separated by HPLC measurement, which removed approximately 0.0002 L and interrupted the operation stream. A replay that omits the intermediate measurement is operationally similar but not identical. This procedural detail limits how literally the sealed batch can be translated into a recipe.

There was only one Batch 2 observation. Therefore, its repeatability, variance, and sensitivity to small control deviations are unknown. The temperature comparison suggests that the 400 K region is preferable to 410–420 K for balance, but it does not locate a sharp optimum. The duration comparison was conducted at 410 K rather than 400 K, so the best 400 K duration was not directly mapped.

A proper repeatability test would run multiple randomized, independently initialized replicas of the exact Batch 2 lifecycle, including either consistently retaining or consistently omitting the intermediate HPLC measurement. It would compare full final-assay distributions, actual thermal histories, peak risk, and failure frequency rather than only average score.

Local robustness should be tested with a small response surface around the recommendation, for example 395, 400, and 405 K crossed with several durations around 2700–3900 s. Small variations in catalyst amount, solvent volume, and stirring would determine whether the result lies on a broad plateau or a fragile ridge. Replication at the center would separate curvature from noise.

Cross-material generalization would require repeating that local design with at least the strongest alternative catalyst and solvent categories. The campaign showed that catalyst and solvent rankings matter, but it did not establish that their effects are additive or invariant across temperature. Generalization to real materials is not justified because the catalysts and kinetic solvent effects were anonymous benchmark calibrations.

Cross-world generalization would require independent world instances or seeds using the same public protocol, with the recommendation judged by predictive coverage and regret relative to each world's local optimum. Nothing in the present campaign proves that the same latent rate hierarchy persists across worlds.

The correct final distinction is therefore: Batch 12 was the numerically highest-scoring sample in this one campaign; Batch 2 was the selected, more interpretable operating recommendation; and neither condition was proven globally optimal, locally unique, or even superior in expectation without replication.

recommendation.selection_rationale: Catalyst D in water at a 400 K requested boundary for 3300 s with prompt quench gave the cleanest direct high-yield operating result: yield 0.773, selectivity 0.822, low degradation, and safety risk 0.075, well below the 0.35 limit. The slightly higher score of batch 12 was not a resolved quench-timing effect.
